item.title: The Painter the Art World Loves to Forget
item.description: Artist, novelist, playwright, wrestler, fashion muse — the Rosalyn Drexler rediscovery is on (again).
item.dc:creator: Jillian Steinhauer

item.title: Chicano, Gay and Still Inspiring Connections
item.description: At El Museo del Barrio, a survey of the art multitasker Teddy Sandoval and his fictional collective, the Butch Gardens School.
item.dc:creator: Holland Cotter

item.title: A Fresh Take on Rembrandt Is Coming to the Met, Then Heading to the Louvre
item.description: The exhibition, with paintings new to the United States, opens in November 2027. The Met’s Facade and Great Hall commissions go to Danh Vo and Sandra Mujinga.
item.dc:creator: Leila Sheridan

item.title: Sculptors Panic as Specialty Plaster Used in Artworks to Be Discontinued
item.description: Artists are scrambling for alternatives to Hydrocal plaster, a crucial component for making sculptures.
item.dc:creator: Zachary Small

item.title: Connecting the Dots Between Roy Lichtenstein and Today
item.description: The Whitney’s retrospective is full of jokes, but it captures our image overload with surprising tenderness. Our critic calls it “the most momentous exhibition of the season.”
item.dc:creator: Jason Farago
item.media:credit: Marissa Alper for The New York Times
item.media:description: “New York World’s Fair Mural (Girl in Window)” by Roy Lichtenstein, from 1963, has been recreated and hand painted by Alex Da Corte’s studio. At 32 feet tall, on the Whitney’s terrace, it can be seen from the High Line.

item.title: Should Robert Rauschenberg’s Art Studio Be Saved?
item.description: The potential sale of the groundbreaking painter’s home in New York by his foundation, on the heels of the sale of his Florida studio, has alarmed many in the art community.
item.dc:creator: Deborah Solomon

item.title: Artists’ Studios Where Creativity Is on Display
item.description: The studio of the Pop master Tom Wesselmann opened briefly for a peek. Other exhibitions continue at the studios of Donald Judd and Sean Scully.
item.dc:creator: Deborah Solomon

item.title: Are You Prepared for MoMA’s New Swamp?
item.description: The Danish artist Jakob Kudsk Steensen is driven by fascination with wetlands and a penchant for video games. His exhibition presents a mystical, esoteric world.
item.dc:creator: Frank Rose
item.media:credit: Mathias Eis for The New York Times
item.media:description: The Danish artist Jakob Kudsk Steensen at a wetlands near Copenhagen. His work “Berl-Berl,” a game engine-powered digital simulation of the swamp Berlin was built on, will be shown in the Museum of Modern Art’s lobby starting Oct. 12.

item.title: The Fresh Charms of Art From the 15th Century
item.description: At the Met, an exhibition of 16 pieces transports viewers to a place and time when the virtues of artworks were refreshingly different from ours today.
item.dc:creator: Blake Gopnik

item.title: Jeff Koons Is Selling $100 Million of His Personal Art Collection
item.description: Much of the trove, offered this fall at Christie’s, comes from a buying spree in the late 2000s and includes Dutch Golden Age art and paintings by Picasso and Manet.
item.dc:creator: Zachary Small
item.media:description: Jeff Koons, shown at an exhibition of his work, “Lost in America,” in 2021 in Doha, Qatar, will sell nine historic paintings he collected in November at Christie’s, including a Picasso and a Manet.

item.title: Love and Pain Powered the Game-Changing Art of Krasner and Pollock
item.description: Lee Krasner and Jackson Pollock are the focus of a blockbuster show at the Met Museum. Four paintings reveal how their high-intensity relationship became a laboratory for ideas.
item.dc:creator: Amei Wallach

item.title: A Knockout Show Resets the Record With ‘Krasner and Pollock’
item.description: She had to settle for the kitchen as her studio but Lee Krasner finally gets her share of the spotlight at the Metropolitan Museum of Art.
item.dc:creator: Holland Cotter
item.media:credit: Pollock-Krasner Foundation/Artists Rights Society (ARS), New York; Photograph by Yuvraj Khanna for The New York Times
item.media:description: Lee Krasner, “The Seasons,” 1957. Oil and house paint on canvas

item.title: Bought for $30, Gertrude Abercrombie Painting Set Off $1.35 Million Bidding War
item.description: “He saved it from forever being lost,” the auction house said of the person who found a Gertrude Abercrombie painting at an estate sale in Kalamazoo, Mich.
item.dc:creator: Rebecca Chao

item.title: Art Gallery Shows to See in October
item.description: This week in Newly Reviewed, Dawn Chan covers Cho Yong-Ik’s genre-defying twists, Asad Raza’s art for animals, Christopher K. Ho’s modernist candelabra, and a group show of papermakers.
item.dc:creator: Dawn Chan, Jillian Steinhauer and Travis Diehl

item.title: A Paris Museum That’s Wild and a ‘Little Weird’
item.description: Despite its provocative subject matter, the Museum of Hunting and Nature aims to be “a joyful cabinet of curiosities.”
item.dc:creator: Rebecca L. Davis
item.category: Musee de la Chasse et de la Nature
item.media:credit: Dmitry Kostyukov for The New York Times
item.media:description: Musée de la Chasse et de la Nature — the Museum of Hunting and Nature — was founded in 1967 by a married couple who were hunting enthusiasts.

item.title: A Lakeside Italian Villa Restored to Its Original Splendor
item.description: After a Swedish couple returned to Europe from Australia, they found a 19th-century weekend refuge near Como.
item.dc:creator: Kurt Soller and Ramona Elèna Balaban

item.title: Kashmir’s Beauty and Violence Captured in an Exquisite Debut at MoMA
item.description: With layered landscapes, patterns and poetry, Nilima Sheikh portrays the fractures and flash points of modern India.
item.dc:creator: Arthur Lubow
item.media:credit: Yuvraj Khanna for The New York Times
item.media:description: Delights and atrocities are depicted with equal tenderness the show, “Fractured Skies.” At right, a figure carries a lifeless body near a woman weeping red tears; at center, a decapitation in a garden.

item.title: As Big Money Flees London’s Art Scene, Young Galleries Sharpen Their Edge
item.description: Tax reforms and Paris’s rise have taken a toll. But low-budget, risk-taking dealers are still creating buzz at the Frieze London fair and beyond.
item.dc:creator: Scott Reyburn and Sam Bush
item.media:credit: Sam Bush for The New York Times
item.media:description: Self Portrait 91 by Issy Wood on display at the Carlos/Ishikawa booth during Frieze Art Fair in London on Wednesday.

item.title: In His Montmartre Atelier, a Self-Made, 91-Year-Old Artist Paints On
item.description: Henri Landier is so committed to his work that, in the early days, he slept on newspapers in an unheated shack. Now, he has had shows from Japan to India.
item.dc:creator: Elaine Sciolino

item.title: The Artist Boz Deseo Garden and the Afterlife of the Slave Trade
item.description: Boz Deseo Garden, whose work explores the “afterlife” of the trans-Atlantic slave trade, is having their Art Basel Paris debut.
item.dc:creator: Will Higginbotham

item.title: At Art Basel Paris and Beyond, Celebrating 200 Years of Photography
item.description: Several artists at Art Basel Paris are honoring photography’s origins as France hosts hundreds of events to celebrate the medium’s bicentennial.
item.dc:creator: Keridwen Cornelius

item.title: What Else to Check Out During Art Basel Paris
item.description: Marie Antoinette, Cézanne and more await you if you step off the beaten path at the Paris art fair.
item.dc:creator: Farah Nayeri

item.title: For Contemporary Art, the Large Center Is a Big Deal
item.description: The huge art center on Île Seguin near Paris opens with a show of works collected by the automaker Renault and the real estate tycoon Laurent Dumas.
item.dc:creator: Tina Isaac-Goizé
item.media:credit: Dmitry Kostyukov for The New York Times
item.media:description: Large, a contemporary art center on Île Seguin in the Seine, southwest of Paris. The island was once the site of a Renault factory.

item.title: The Thrillingly Intricate Art of Cut Paper
item.description: A new generation is putting a fresh — and sometimes subversive — spin on the ancient practice.
item.dc:creator: Kin Woo and Mari Maeda-Oboshi and Yuji Oboshi

item.title: Engagement Gifts That Can Double as Wedding Presents
item.description: Velvet jewelry trays, keepsake matchboxes and more recommendations from T Magazine.

item.title: Andreas Schulze’s Collection of Spritzdekor Ceramics
item.description: The painter Andreas Schulze shares his collection of hundreds of airbrushed ceramic pieces.
item.dc:creator: Kin Woo

item.title: White Paint. It’s Everywhere. She Hates It.
item.description: In her latest book, “A Dead White,” Wendy S. Walters considers the seemingly neutral background of daily life.
item.dc:creator: Steven Kurutz
item.category: A Dead White: An Argument Against White Paint (Book)
item.media:credit: Daniela Spector for The New York Times
item.media:description: The author, surrounded by the white-painted walls she has come to loathe.

item.title: Celebrating the Enduring Newness of Magritte in London
item.description: A gallery show in London features works by the famously cranky Belgian Surrealist alongside new works by artists he inspired.
item.dc:creator: Dale Berning Sawa

item.title: At Frieze London, the People Who Make It All Work
item.description: Behind the scenes, it takes a small army of players to pull off the art fair. Here is a look at four of them.
item.dc:creator: Shivani Vora
item.media:credit: Jeremie Souteyrat for The New York Times
item.media:description: Kristell Chadé, the executive director of fairs for Frieze. “By the time we open to the public, hundreds of people who visitors never see have already been working for months,” she said.

item.title: Beyond the London Fairs: Even More Art
item.description: The museums and galleries have much to offer those coming to Frieze London.
item.dc:creator: Jillian Rayfield

item.title: Gabriel Orozco Shows New Art In London
item.description: A conversation with Gabriel Orozco, who will be showing a sprawling body of work, both old and new, in London.
item.dc:creator: Farah Nayeri

item.title: Sotheby’s Soars as Galleries Struggle in Britain’s Art World
item.description: As auction houses like Sotheby’s move millions of dollars of art, some high-profile galleries struggle.
item.dc:creator: Farah Nayeri
item.media:credit: Jeremie Souteyrat for The New York Times
item.media:description: Checking out a painting by Pedro Paricio at Halcyon Gallery in London. Recently, some of the city’s major galleries have struggled, with Stephen Friedman Gallery and Tiwani Contemporary closing earlier this year.

item.title: In the Shadows of the Art World, an Invisible Industry Operates
item.description: Right now, hundreds of artworks worth millions are making their way across the world. These people make the travel arrangements.
item.dc:creator: Mercedes Hutton
item.media:credit: Lam Yik Fei for The New York Times
item.media:description: Staff members at the Hong Kong office of Eythos, an art logistics company, wrapped an artwork in the framing room.

item.title: Frieze London: Bringing Attention to Art From the Middle East
item.description: A Saudi gallery will be making its Frieze London debut, showcasing two artists from the region.
item.dc:creator: David Belcher

item.title: Frieze London: A 72-year-old Artist Makes Her Debut
item.description: Kaye Brown, a retired teacher, didn’t pick up a paintbrush until 2012. Her works depict the body-painting designs Tiwi people wear in mourning.
item.dc:creator: Vivian Morelli

item.title: The Andrew Edmunds Collection Is for Sale at Frieze Masters
item.description: The Andrew Edmunds collection, which comprises more than 10,000 prints and drawings will be on sale at Frieze Masters.

item.media:description: An original, hand-colored example of “The Plumb-pudding in danger” showing Napoleon, right, and William Pitt the Younger by James Gillray, from the Andrew Edmunds collection.
